questions.q: What is the threshold voltage of an N-channel enhancement-mode MOSFET?

options.A: The largest voltage the drain can withstand.
options.B: The smallest gate–source voltage at which it starts to conduct between drain and source.
options.C: The voltage across the load when it is switched on.
options.D: The supply voltage of the circuit.

questions.solution: Below the threshold voltage the MOSFET is off, with only a tiny leakage current. Once the gate–source voltage rises above the threshold, a conducting channel forms and current can flow between the drain and the source.

questions.q: Why can a MOSFET be driven directly by a sensor that can supply only a very small current?

options.A: Its gate has a very high input resistance, so it draws almost no current.
options.B: Its gate has a very low input resistance, so it draws a large current.
options.C: It amplifies the sensor's voltage before switching.

questions.solution: The gate is insulated from the channel by a thin oxide layer, so the input resistance is extremely high and almost no gate current flows. A small voltage from the sensor is enough to switch a large current through the load.

questions.q: How is a zener diode used to provide a constant voltage?

options.A: In forward bias, in parallel with the supply and with no resistor.
options.B: In forward bias, in series with a resistor.
options.C: In reverse bias, connected directly across the supply.
options.D: In reverse bias, in series with a resistor, with the output taken across the diode.

questions.solution: Above its breakdown voltage in reverse bias, the voltage across a zener diode stays almost constant over a wide range of current. A series resistor drops the rest of the supply voltage and limits the current. The steady output is taken across the diode.

questions.q: A 5.1 V zener diode is in series with a \(130\ \Omega\) resistor across a 9.0 V supply. What is the current in the resistor?
questions.solution: The diode holds 5.1 V, so the resistor has 9.0 − 5.1 = 3.9 V across it. Current = 3.9 ÷ 130 = 0.030 A. Using the whole supply voltage (0.069 A) is the usual slip.

questions.q: How is a photodiode connected and used in photo-conductive mode?

options.A: Forward biased, giving out light when a current flows.
options.B: Forward biased, with a current that does not depend on light.
options.C: Reverse biased, with a current that increases with light intensity.
options.D: Unconnected, storing charge when light falls on it.

questions.solution: In photo-conductive mode the photodiode is reverse biased. In the dark only a tiny current flows. Light releases charge carriers in the junction, giving a reverse current proportional to the light intensity, and the response is fast enough for optical communication.

questions.q: What does a Hall effect sensor detect?
questions.solution: A Hall effect sensor gives an output voltage that depends on the magnetic flux density through it. It can count the turns of a shaft carrying a small magnet (a tachometer), or sense orientation relative to the Earth's field.

questions.q: How many different quantisation levels can a 4-bit sample represent?
questions.solution: Each bit doubles the number of values. The number of levels for 4 bits is two multiplied by itself four times: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.

questions.q: An audio signal contains frequencies up to 15 kHz. What is the lowest sampling rate that can reproduce it?
questions.solution: The sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in the signal, or the high frequencies are lost or misread. Minimum rate = 2 × 15 = 30 kHz.

questions.q: A parallel LC circuit has an inductance of 1.0 mH and a capacitance of \(1.0\ \mu\text{F}\). What is its resonant frequency?
questions.solution: \(f_{0} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}\). Here \(\sqrt{1.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-6}} = 3.16 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{s}\), so the resonant frequency is 5000 Hz, which is 5.0 kHz. Leaving out the \(2\pi\) (32 kHz) is the usual slip.

questions.q: An LC filter has a resonant frequency of 10 kHz and a bandwidth of 500 Hz. What is its Q factor?
questions.solution: \(Q = \frac{f_{0}}{f_{B}}\), with both in the same unit: 10 000 ÷ 500 = 20. A higher Q factor means a sharper, more selective filter.

questions.q: An inverting amplifier has a feedback resistor of \(47\ \text{k}\Omega\) and an input resistor of \(4.7\ \text{k}\Omega\). The input voltage is +0.10 V. What is the output voltage?
questions.solution: \(\frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = -\frac{R_{f}}{R_{in}}\). The resistor ratio is 47 ÷ 4.7, a gain of ten times with the sign reversed. So the output has a size of 1.0 V and is negative: −1.0 V.

questions.q: A non-inverting amplifier has a feedback resistor of \(20\ \text{k}\Omega\) and a resistor of \(10\ \text{k}\Omega\) from the inverting input to 0 V. What is its voltage gain?
questions.solution: \(\frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = 1 + \frac{R_{f}}{R_{1}} = 1 + \frac{20}{10}\) = 3.0. Forgetting to add the one (2.0) is the usual slip.

questions.q: In an inverting amplifier, what is meant by a virtual earth?

options.A: The output is connected to 0 V.
options.B: The power supply is earthed for safety.
options.C: The input signal is always zero.
options.D: The inverting input stays at almost 0 V, although it is not connected to earth.

questions.solution: The non-inverting input is at 0 V, and the open-loop gain is so large that the two inputs must be at almost the same voltage for the output not to saturate. So the inverting input sits at practically 0 V without being connected to earth. This is the basis of virtual-earth analysis.

questions.q: An operational amplifier is used as a comparator. The voltage at its non-inverting input is higher than at its inverting input. What is its output?

options.A: Close to the positive supply voltage.
options.B: Close to the negative supply voltage.
options.D: Equal to the difference between the two inputs.

questions.solution: With no feedback, the tiny difference between the inputs is multiplied by the huge open-loop gain, so the output saturates. It goes close to the positive supply when the non-inverting input is higher, and close to the negative supply when it is lower.

questions.q: Which two-input logic gate gives an output of 1 only when both inputs are 0?
questions.solution: A NOR gate is an OR gate followed by a NOT gate. OR gives 0 only when both inputs are 0, so NOR gives 1 only then. NAND gives 1 for every input except both being 1.

questions.q: An amplitude-modulated signal carries information with a maximum frequency of 5.0 kHz. What bandwidth does it need?
questions.solution: An AM signal has sidebands on both sides of the carrier, each as wide as the highest information frequency. Bandwidth = 2 × 5.0 = 10 kHz.
